opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about a lot, partly because of GPQA, where the whole design premise was that you could use human expertise as a proxy for difficulty. We had PhD-level domain experts write questions, and then we checked that skilled non-experts with unrestricted web access couldn't answer them even after spending a long time. The gap between expert and non-expert performance was the signal that a question really required deep domain knowledge.

I think human expertise is a useful but quite leaky measure. It works reasonably well as a first approximation because a lot of what makes something hard for humans, like needing a lot of specialized knowledge or many steps of careful reasoning, also tends to make it hard for models. But the correlation is much weaker than people often assume. Models have a very different capability profile from humans. They've read basically the entire internet, so tasks that are hard for humans mainly because they require recalling obscure facts can be relatively easy for a model. Meanwhile, tasks a human finds trivial, like keeping track of state over a long interaction, noticing that something has gone wrong and backing up, or operating in a messy real-world environment, can be surprisingly hard for models.

So I've moved more toward thinking about difficulty in terms of things like how long a task takes a skilled human to complete. That's the idea behind the time horizon work at METR. We measure how long tasks take human professionals and then look at the length of task where a model succeeds some fraction of the time. Time to complete isn't a perfect measure either, but it seems to capture something important: longer tasks need more sustained coherence, more error correction, more planning, and those seem to be where models still struggle relative to people. Empirically, it also gives you a surprisingly clean trend over time, which suggests it's tracking something real.

The broader point is that "how hard is this for an expert human" and "how hard is this for an AI system" are related but different questions, and if we lean too heavily on the first, we can be misled in both directions. We might overestimate a model because it aces an exam that's hard for humans, or underestimate how far it is from doing useful autonomous work because the things it fails at seem easy to us.

r001.rationale: It calls human expertise a “useful but quite leaky measure” and says its correlation with model difficulty is weaker than often assumed.

r002.rationale: It contrasts exam performance with difficulties in autonomous work, but does not clearly identify agency as a greater bottleneck than advanced problem-solving.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says operating in a “messy real-world environment” can be surprisingly hard for models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that it's a pretty imperfect proxy, but it's one of the better ones we have, and I've spent a lot of time thinking about why.

The basic intuition is something like: if a task requires someone to have a PhD in organic chemistry, or to have spent ten years practicing law, that's a signal that the task is hard, because humans had to invest a lot to be able to do it. And there's a loose correlation there. Things that require a lot of specialized human training tend to involve long chains of reasoning, lots of background knowledge, and judgment calls that are hard to specify. So when we were building GPQA, part of the motivation was exactly this. We wanted questions where domain experts could get them right, but where very smart, very motivated non-experts with full internet access couldn't, even given a lot of time. That gap between expert and skilled non-expert felt like a meaningful thing to measure, because it tells you the question isn't just lookup, it actually requires the expertise.

But I think there are a couple of ways the proxy breaks down, and they break in opposite directions.

One is that human difficulty and AI difficulty just aren't the same thing. There are tasks that are trivially easy for humans, like persistently working on something over a week, noticing when you've gone down a wrong path, keeping track of a bunch of loosely related context, and those have been really hard for models. And conversely, there are things that are hard for humans mostly because of memory or breadth, like knowing a fact from every subfield of biology at once, and those are almost free for a model. So "requires an expert" sometimes means "requires a lot of accumulated knowledge," which is a thing models are specifically good at, and sometimes means "requires a kind of taste or judgment that takes years to develop," which is a much more interesting thing to test. Human expertise bundles those together and doesn't tell you which one you're getting.

The second problem is more practical. Once you're at the frontier of human expertise, your ability to even evaluate the task gets really shaky. If you want questions that only the top experts in a field can answer, you need those experts to write them, and other experts to validate them, and when they disagree, you don't have a ground truth to appeal to. We saw this on GPQA, where a nontrivial fraction of the disagreements between experts were basically about whether the question was well-posed, not about the answer. And that's at the PhD-student level. If you push further, toward actual open research questions, the whole idea of a benchmark with a known answer starts to fall apart, because by definition nobody knows the answer. So human expertise is useful as a measure right up until the point where it's most interesting, and then it stops being usable.

So where I've landed is that expertise is a reasonable way to generate hard tasks and to sanity check them, but I try not to treat "expert-level" as a fixed threshold that means anything specific about capability. What I care about more is the structure of the task. How long is it, how much does it require correcting your own mistakes, how much is verifiable versus requiring judgment. Those feel like they track the things that actually matter for whether a model can do useful or dangerous work in the world, and human expertise is just one noisy input into that.

r001.rationale: The response calls human expertise an imperfect proxy and explains that human and AI difficulty can diverge.

r002.rationale: It notes that persistence, self-correction, and context tracking are hard for models, but does not identify agency as a greater bottleneck than advanced expertise.

r003.rationale: It mentions loosely related context and long tasks, but does not clearly identify sensitivity to messy task conditions as a bottleneck.

astra-6.text:
I think human expertise is a useful proxy, but you have to be careful about what it’s a proxy for. Something that takes a person years of training to do isn’t necessarily going to be harder for an AI system than something that people do effortlessly. There’s no guarantee that the ordering of difficulty is the same.

But expertise does give us a practical way to find tasks that might challenge current systems. If you ask questions that someone without relevant training can answer, you may run out of room to measure progress pretty quickly. Questions that require specialized knowledge can give you more room, and experts can help judge whether the answers are actually right.

So I’d distinguish ‘this is difficult for humans’ from ‘we’ve measured that this is difficult for AI.’ The first is a useful starting point for constructing an evaluation. It doesn’t substitute for the second.

r001.rationale: The response says human expertise is only a useful proxy and that the human and AI difficulty orderings are not guaranteed to match.

r002.rationale: It does not identify agency as a greater bottleneck than solving advanced problems.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss sensitivity to messy task conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think human expertise is a useful starting point, but it’s a pretty imperfect proxy. If a question requires years of specialized training for a human to answer, that gives us some reason to think it might be challenging for an AI system. But humans and AI systems don’t necessarily find the same things difficult. A model might have encountered an answer many times in its training data, even if learning to produce that answer would take a human a long time.

There’s also a distinction between knowing a lot about a subject and being able to reason through a new problem in that subject. So I’d want to use expertise to help us construct candidate tasks, and then actually test whether those tasks are difficult for the systems we care about. The fact that an expert can answer a question and a nonexpert can’t is informative, but it doesn’t by itself establish that the question measures some capability an AI system lacks.

r001.rationale: It calls human expertise an imperfect proxy and explains that humans and AI systems can find different things difficult.

r002.rationale: It does not identify agency as a greater bottleneck than solving problems requiring advanced human expertise.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss sensitivity to messy task conditions as a bottleneck for modern AI systems.
